source.title: Treasury Management Annual Outturn Report and Prudential Indicators 2025/26 — Audit Committee, 30 June 2026, agenda item 11

facts.note: The covering paper carries the recommendation, cycle framing and administrative sections only. Every table, indicator and rate lives in Appendix A (72890, 17pp), which is on disk and read here in full. Both citations below use 72890 page numbers unless stated.

source.title: Appendix A, Table 3 (p.9), Table 8 (p.14) and para 6.9.7

facts.note: Verbatim para 6.9.7: 'There was no debt held by the council during 2025/2026.' Verbatim para 3.1: 'Hertsmere currently do not have any external borrowing.' The Operational Boundary (£70m) and Authorised Limit (£75m) both stood against £0m actual (Table 8, p.14).

Table 6 arithmetic: £21,769 b/fwd + £8,673 new financing − £851 principal repayments − £3,290 MRP/VRP = £26,301. Consistent. Actual outturn CFR £26.301m against an Original Estimate of £19.051m is a £7.25m overshoot; the movement is capital-financed and comes largely from a £2.800m VRP raised against the HLL Clarendon Road and St Johns loans (para 6.6). Table 3 on p.9 prints CFR £21.7m at the same date — the Table 3 row is out of date and inconsistent with the Table 6 arithmetic. Table 6 is the authoritative figure.

Verbatim: 'Whilst the CFR shows that the Council has a need to borrow of £26.301m this continues to be funded by utilisation of cash balances or internal borrowing.' No PFI, no finance leases and no other long-term liabilities are disclosed in the paper. Balance-sheet identity: CFR £26.301m − external £0 − OLTL £0 = internal £26.301m. TIES.

facts.value: £73.9m at 31 March 2026 (2024/25: £67.9m). Core investments £58.0m at 4.44%; capital & working-capital loans £15.9m at 6.28%; combined 4.77%.
facts.note: Both core life <1yr, capital/working-capital life >1yr. Table 4 (p.10) gives the average balance for the year at £68.681m at 4.44% on core, and states actual investment income was £3.714m against a budget of £1.500m — a £2.213m overshoot on the general fund alone.

facts.value: £50m of the £58m core investment book at 31 March 2026 is Other Local Authority lending — 86.2% of core, 67.7% of the full £73.9m
facts.note: Verbatim Note 2: 'Includes £6.1m in Money Market Fund investments, £1.9m in Barclays Instant Access BPA, and £50m Other Local Authority lending.' Cross-references para 2.2 (p.4): 'Average investment returns across the year for the Council remained robust at around 4.79% ... aided by continuation of elevated rates of return from inter authority lending particularly.' Also para 2.6 (p.5): 'Investment balances have been kept to a minimum through the agreed strategy of using reserves and balances to support internal borrowing, rather than borrowing externally from the financial markets.' Hertsmere is a lender into the LA-to-LA market; across the library we see the borrower side (e.g. Broxbourne, Wiltshire, Cherwell) and other lenders (Wandsworth £235m).

Verbatim 6.8.2: 'Financing costs are negative as the Council has no external debt and hence the investment income is greater than the interest payable.' A net earner. The 2025/26 outturn is more negative than budget by 13.49pp, driven by the £2.213m investment-income overshoot in Table 4.

facts.value: £15.984m of related-party loans at 31 March 2026 across five recipients, weighted 6.28% (matches Table 3's £15.9m)
facts.note: Composition: InspireAll £2.602m at 5% (renegotiated 2023); Hertsmere Developments Ltd £0.5m at UK base+4% (£0.7m repaid in year against a £1.2m facility); Hertsmere Living Ltd £2.0m 40-year annuity at 6.22% (Clarendon Road, drawn March 2024 — 'equivalent to the then PWLB rate plus 1%') plus £0.8m 40-year annuity at 6.68% (St Johns); Elstree Film Studio £10.0m working-capital facility at UK base+2% (facility fully drawn as at March 2026); Hertfordshire Building Control £0.082m at 6% (moving to base+2% from April 2026). An MRP of £0.500m on EFS starts 2026/27 (para 2.16).

facts.value: 3.75% at 31 March 2026 (three 0.25% cuts through 2025/26; MUFG holds 3.75% through March 2027)
facts.note: MUFG forecast: Bank Rate held at 3.75% to March 2027, then 3.50% Sep 2027, 3.25% Dec 2027 and hold to March 2029. Capital Economics has 3.00% by Dec 2027. Adviser is MUFG (named at para 2.3 and background documents section).

Certainty rates as the paper prints them. Recorded for completeness; Hertsmere holds no PWLB debt so these rates are contextual only, not directly applicable to any repricing exposure. Rate move since (14 Aug 2026 PM, DMO notice 314/26 PM): 5y +0.06pp, 10y +0.11pp, 25y +0.17pp — small drift up at the long end.

facts.value: £8.474m actual against a revised restated budget of £28.214m — a £19.740m undelivered slice
facts.note: None of the £8.474m actual was financed by external borrowing (the original budget had £7.264m of internal borrowing, revised to £4.068m, actual £0). Financing came from Capital Receipts £2.971m, Capital Grants £1.487m, DFG £0.952m, Earmarked Reserve £0.790m and S106/CIL £2.274m. The mismatch between planned and actual capital delivery is part of the reason investment balances trended higher through 2025/26.

signals.headline: Zero external borrowing, £26.301m CFR entirely internal, £73.9m of investments (£50m of which is Other Local Authority lending), and a ratio of financing costs to net revenue of (25.22)% — Hertsmere is a net earner at 31 March 2026
signals.why_it_matters: There is no refinancing risk to price, no LOBO exposure, no PWLB book to repay early. The story worth writing about is the composition of the investment side (86% of core in inter-authority lending) and the sub-book of related-party loans (£15.984m across five recipients at 5%–6.68%). No distress signal; a clean quiet outturn.

summary.text:
The paper for the 30 June 2026 Audit Committee is a three-page covering report (72889) with every treasury figure held in a seventeen-page Appendix A (72890). Both are on disk and read here. The read is straightforward and the shape is distinctive.

Hertsmere holds no external borrowing. Total debt is £0.0m at both 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026 (Table 3, p.9; Table 8, p.14; para 6.9.7 states 'There was no debt held by the council during 2025/2026'). The Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2026 is £26.301m (Table 6, p.12; para 6.5) — the whole CFR is funded internally, corroborated verbatim at para 6.7. The balance-sheet identity ties: £26.301m − £0 − £0 = £26.301m of internal borrowing, with no PFI or finance-lease liabilities disclosed. The PWLB loan-book reconciliation ties by absence: our price-book returns no borrower under 'Hertsmere' or 'Hertsmere Borough', matching the paper's £0 external. There is nothing to tie in the email as a match; both sides say zero.

On the other side, the council holds £73.9m of investments at 31 March 2026 (Table 3, p.9). The core £58.0m is 86.2% in Other Local Authority lending (£50m of £58m per Table 11 Note 2, p.16), with £6.1m in Money Market Funds and £1.9m in a Barclays Instant Access BPA. Weighted return on core 4.44%; combined return with capital and working-capital loans of £15.9m at 6.28%, the whole book yields 4.77%. Actual investment income for the year was £3.714m against a budget of £1.500m — a £2.213m overshoot (Table 4, p.10). The ratio of financing costs to net revenue is (25.22)% actual against (11.73)% budget and (20.68)% prior year (Table 7, p.13) — Hertsmere is a net earner, more negative than budget by 13.49 percentage points.

A distinct sub-book of related-party loans totals £15.984m across five recipients (paras 2.7–2.17): InspireAll £2.602m at 5%; Hertsmere Developments Ltd £0.5m at base+4%; Hertsmere Living Ltd £2.0m at 6.22% (Clarendon Road, 40-year annuity drawn March 2024 at 'the then PWLB rate plus 1%') plus £0.8m at 6.68% (St Johns); Elstree Film Studio £10.0m at base+2% (facility fully drawn); Hertfordshire Building Control £0.082m at 6%. An MRP of £0.500m on EFS begins 2026/27 (para 2.16). This sums to £15.984m — matches Table 3's £15.9m to rounding.

An email is drafted. The reconciliation ties by absence and there is no PWLB book to price, but the paper carries a strong hook: at £50m of the £58m core, Hertsmere is a substantial lender into the inter-authority market — a market we see the other side of every month across the library (Broxbourne borrows about £51.65m into it, Wandsworth lends £235m into it). The draft opens on that concentration and the shape of what we see from the other side, offers the (25.22)% net-earner framing as context, and points at the pwlb-activity page. No advice, no recommendations. The S151 email address is published on the paper's front sheet (Matthew Bunyon, matthew.bunyon@hertsmere.gov.uk) so this is 'ready to send' state.

[INTERNAL ONLY] Table 3 (p.9) prints CFR £21.7m at 31 March 2026 while Table 6 (p.12) prints £26.301m with self-consistent arithmetic and para 6.5 uses £26.301m. Table 3's CFR row is stale — likely populated before Table 6 was finalised. Not raised with the council; recorded here for the loop.

officer.body:
Dear Matthew,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Treasury Outturn taken to Audit Committee on 30 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. It's a clean report and the covering paper does a lot with three pages, which made it a straightforward read alongside Appendix A.

One thing worth saying upfront. Our loan file holds no PWLB debt for Hertsmere, which matches the £0.0m at Table 3 and Table 8 and paragraph 6.9.7. So the usual opening of this email, a loan-book reconciliation, has nothing to reconcile. The balance-sheet identity ties on the paper's own figures — CFR £26.301m, external £0, other long-term liabilities £0, internal borrowing £26.301m, exactly as your paragraph 6.7 sets out.

The thing that caught our eye is Table 11 Note 2. Of the £58m core investment book at 31 March, £50m is with other local authorities — 86% of the core, and about two thirds of the whole £73.9m if you include the capital and working-capital loans. Table 4 shows the £68.681m average balance yielded 4.44% on core against Bank Rate of 3.75%, and paragraph 2.2 attributes the position to 'continuation of elevated rates of return from inter authority lending particularly'. That is a distinct shape — a substantial LA-to-LA lender rather than a marginal one.

Here is why it might be interesting to you. We read the borrower side of that market too. Broxbourne, just up the road, has a £51.65m debt portfolio that is entirely short-dated inter-authority money maturing April to September this year, priced roughly at Bank Rate. Wandsworth is a much bigger lender on the same side as you at £235m and has published unusually candid appendices on the pricing spread they see. Cherwell, Wiltshire and Herefordshire show single-loan rates from about 4.15% at the bottom to 7% at the top depending on when in the month the counterparty came looking. Nobody publishes this market, so every council sees only its own trades — the reason the same week can produce very different rates. We track that pricing across the sector alongside the PWLB curve at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and it is the page most relevant to a book shaped like yours.

On the affordability side, Table 7 is worth flagging back only because it is unusual. The ratio of financing costs to net revenue came in at (25.22)% actual against a (11.73)% budget — meaning investment income exceeded interest payable by that much. Paragraph 6.8.2 explains it plainly and it is a coherent position: no external debt, £2.213m investment surplus against budget (Table 4), and a net earner. It is a distinctive shape among the outturns we have read this summer and one worth having a name for when it comes to member briefings — most councils in the file are on the positive side of that ratio, some materially so.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151. The liability benchmark — a projection of what a council's external debt would need to be to leave a minimum cash cushion — becomes central. For a council carrying £26.301m of internal borrowing against £73.9m of investments, most of which is short-dated LA lending, the pathway that comes out of it is what would tell you when internal capacity starts to bind and whether any external drawing becomes economic. We do not price break costs on a book that is £0, so nothing to say there.

On training, three fit the paper. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets picks up the concentration in Table 11 Note 2 directly. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice covers the point above. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting is the discipline behind a portfolio that is mostly short-dated and largely one counterparty type. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
